ECE 6390

The FFT frequency grid

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows the same Gaussian-pulse spectrum stored in native FFT order and then reordered by fftshift so zero frequency sits in the middle.

Sampling a pulse N times at interval Δt gives a sampling rate fₛ = 1/Δt and a Fourier-bin spacing Δf = fₛ/N = 1/(NΔt). The unnormalized discrete Fourier transform Xₖ = Σ pₙe^(−j2πkn/N) returns N values, one per bin. Multiplying by Δt turns the sum into a Riemann-sum approximation of the continuous transform, P(fₖ) ≈ Δt·Xₖ, with units of volt-seconds for a voltage pulse.

Native FFT storage starts at zero frequency, runs through the positive frequencies and then stores the negative ones: for even N, index k represents kΔf when k < N/2 and (k − N)Δf when k ≥ N/2. Bin k = N/2 is the Nyquist frequency ±fₛ/2. Applying fftshift to both the frequency vector and the transform moves the negative half in front, so zero frequency sits in the centre. It rearranges the same numbers without changing any of them.

Two choices set the grid. A longer record, a larger NΔt, gives finer true frequency resolution. A shorter Δt raises fₛ and widens the range of frequencies the samples can represent; a pulse too narrow for its Δt aliases. Zero padding before the FFT appends samples of value zero, so it plots more points on the same underlying spectrum without improving resolution.

These conventions matter whenever an FFT checks a pulse against a spectral mask or computes an aperture pattern: plotting values against bin index, or forgetting the Δt scale, gives wrong frequencies or wrong magnitudes.

Example

With N = 64 samples at Δt = 0.05 s, fₛ = 20 Hz and Δf = 0.3125 Hz. Bin k = 10 represents 3.125 Hz, while bin k = 54 represents (54 − 64) × 0.3125 = −3.125 Hz. After fftshift, zero frequency moves to position 32.

Practice

1. For N = 128 samples at Δt = 1 ms, what are fₛ and Δf, and which frequency does bin k = 100 represent?

Use fₛ = 1/Δt and Δf = fₛ/N; bins at or above N/2 hold negative frequencies.

fₛ = 1000 Hz and Δf = 7.8125 Hz. Bin 100 is at least 64, so it represents (100 − 128) × 7.8125 = −218.75 Hz.

2. Does zero-padding a 64-sample record to 256 samples separate two tones 0.1 Hz apart when Δf was 0.3125 Hz?

Separate the plotted grid spacing from the length of the measured record.

No. Padding plots the spectrum on a 0.078 Hz grid, but the measured record is still 3.2 s long, so the resolution stays near 1/3.2 s ≈ 0.31 Hz. Only a longer measurement separates the tones.
